# Purpose of This Document

This is a management summary, not a specification. It reports whether the
S6/b testing-mode implementation actually behaves as `technology/consensus-transition.md`
and `analysis/Rincoin_840k_S6B_Consensus_Change_Specification.qmd` say it
should — checked by running it, not by re-reading the design. The full
evidence — every test case, raw logs, exact commits — is in
[`S6B/`](S6B/), not repeated here.

This scenario's testing-mode branch was built by branching directly from
the already-tested `consensus/s1-testing` branch and reusing its shared
infrastructure (coinbase commitment, `sig_fork_id`, mainnet blocker, wallet/
PSBT signing) unmodified. Unlike S5/b, S6/b's schedule needed a genuine new
design decision, not just a new formula — see "A Design Decision, Reviewed
Before Implementing" below.

# What Changes at H1, Briefly

At block height 840,000 (mainnet), three things change together: the block
subsidy schedule, a scheduled coinbase commitment identifying the chosen
schedule, and a sighash-level replay identifier (`sig_fork_id`) mixed into
new transaction signatures. The commitment and `sig_fork_id` mechanisms are
identical across every candidate scenario; only the subsidy schedule
differs. S6/b's schedule: four fixed-value phases (4, 2, 1, 0.6 RIN) at
heights 840,000 / 2,100,000 / 4,200,000 / 6,300,000, followed by a hard
cutoff to exactly zero at height 234,587,500 — a height *derived* from an
exact 168,000,000 RIN issuance ceiling, not a designed round number. Full
rationale and byte-level specification:
`analysis/Rincoin_840k_S6B_Consensus_Change_Specification.qmd`. This
document assumes that design and tests it; it does not re-argue it.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{figures/s6b_subsidy_curve.png}
\caption{Maximum permitted block subsidy under the S6/b candidate. Unlike
S1/S5/b, this schedule has no exponential decay to sample densely -- it is
exactly five flat segments, transcribed directly from the specification and
cross-checked against \texttt{analysis/data/S6B\_normative\_test\_vectors.csv}
and \texttt{analysis/scripts/verify\_s6b\_independently.py}.}
\end{figure}
```

# A Design Decision, Reviewed Before Implementing

S1's and S5/b's subsidy formulas are closed-form (a recursive rule, a
binary-shift rule) — the C++ function that computes them is a few lines of
arithmetic. S6/b has no closed form: it's four fixed values over four
height ranges, then a cutoff. Before writing that function, and at the
user's explicit request, a structurally similar existing implementation was
reviewed for lessons: `rincoin-core/rincoin@v1.1`'s own "Customized
Halving" subsidy code (a different, independently developed fork — one
associated with a rival replay-protection proposal
`technology/response-to-rip-0009.md` already responds to, not a neutral
reference).

**What was good, and adopted**: that code expresses its phase boundaries as
multiples of `nSubsidyHalvingInterval` rather than hardcoded mainnet
heights, so mainnet and fast test networks share one code path with
proportionally scaled timing. This directly solves the "how do you make a
228-million-block terminal phase reachable in a regtest functional test"
problem this scenario has to solve. This branch's own `ForkSubsidyPhases`
entries are expressed relative to `ForkH1Height` for the same reason.

**What was not adopted**: that code is a hardcoded, descending `if`/`else
if` chain with bare magic numbers, and — the more important finding — it
has **no terminal cutoff at all**. Its last phase pays 0.6 RIN forever,
confirmed from the very first commit that introduced it, making its total
issuance unbounded. S6/b's own specification derives an exact terminal
height specifically so issuance is bounded to exactly 168,000,000 RIN.
Both call themselves "Scenario II"; they are not the same rule. Adopting
that code's shape as-is would have silently implemented a different,
unbounded scenario.

**What was built instead**: `Consensus::Params::ForkSubsidyPhases`, a
plain, ordered, variable-length table of `{offset_from_h1, subsidy}`
entries, populated per network in `chainparams.cpp`. `GetBlockSubsidyPostFork()`
is a generic scan over this table — nothing in it is specific to having
exactly four phases. Extending or changing the schedule later is a data
change to the table, not a rewrite of validation logic.

# Summary

**Every test that has been run passes.** 532 of 532 C++ unit tests, 159 of
159 functional tests, and every cross-implementation comparison run so
far — on the first attempt, with no fix cycle needed (unlike S5/b, whose
test suite needed a real fix for a structural MWEB-height interaction).

{{< include includes/s6b_results_summary_table.qmd >}}

Two evidence layers are not yet complete, both inherited from S1 rather
than newly discovered here — see Results §5.4 and
[`S6B/open-items.md`](S6B/open-items.md).

# Methods: What Was Tested, and How

Four groups, used consistently through both this section and Results — the
same four used for S1 and S5/b:

| Group | What it checks | Why it's a separate group |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit-level | Each piece of consensus logic against frozen, byte-exact vectors | Smallest testable unit; catches an error before it can reach anything that depends on it |
| Single-node functional | The same rules, enforced end-to-end by a real running node via RPC/P2P | Confirms the rules hold when driven the way a real deployment would drive them |
| Multi-node functional | Whether the network prefers higher work only when that chain is also rule-valid | The core guarantee the coinbase-commitment mechanism exists to provide |
| Cross-implementation | What happens when this build meets software that disagrees with it | The only layer that reflects the network as it actually is |

## Unit-level

The subsidy phase table is checked against `analysis/data/S6B_normative_test_vectors.csv`
(every phase boundary and the terminal cutoff) and independently against
`analysis/scripts/verify_s6b_independently.py`, a pre-existing script that
derives the terminal height from the issuance ceiling without importing the
C++ implementation — reused directly rather than duplicated, since it
already does exactly what S1's and S5/b's own from-scratch re-derivation
scripts do for their scenarios. The commitment builder/parser and
`sig_fork_id` sighash-mixing code are reused unmodified from
`consensus/s1-testing`.

## Single-node functional

Driven through a real, running `rincoind` process via its actual RPC and
P2P interfaces: coinbase-commitment validation (reused unmodified from S1),
and subsidy enforcement across all five phases of the regtest table,
including the terminal zero phase — see Results §5.2 for why this scenario
could test more of its own schedule directly than S1 or S5/b could.

## Multi-node functional

Reused unmodified from S1: two testing-mode nodes, one isolated to mine a
commitment-valid and a commitment-invalid competing chain; which one is
adopted is the test.

## Cross-implementation

Every accessible node binary tested as both block *producer* and block
*validator* against every other binary.

Same outstanding item as S1 and S5/b: `test/fork_interop_matrix.py` is not

:::

# Results: Did It Pass?

## Unit-level — pass

532 of 532 C++ unit tests pass. The subsidy phase table matches the
specification's own normative vectors at every boundary and at the derived
terminal cutoff:

{{< include includes/s6b_vector_spotcheck_table.qmd >}}

The pre-existing independent verification script confirms the terminal
height and issuance ceiling exactly:

```
Independent S6/b verification passed: first zero height 234,587,500; exact maximum 168,000,000 RIN.
```

The commitment-parsing vector catalog carries the same two open exceptions
S1's and S5/b's own annexes track (not new to this scenario): see
[`S6B/commitment-test-vectors.md`](S6B/commitment-test-vectors.md).

Full detail: [`S6B/unit-test-results.md`](S6B/unit-test-results.md).

## Single-node functional — pass

All commitment-validation checks pass, reused unmodified from S1. Subsidy
enforcement was tested across **all five** phase transitions in this
scenario's regtest table — including the terminal zero cutoff itself, not
just one later boundary — because S6/b's own small-scale table happens to
stay well under the regtest MWEB activation height across its entire
range, unlike S5/b's second boundary. This is meaningfully stronger
coverage than either S1's or S5/b's own subsidy tests, which each only
exercise two data points.

## Multi-node functional — pass

Both reorg outcomes are correct, reusing S1's own mechanism test unmodified.

## Cross-implementation — partially done, passing so far

The full producer × validator matrix has not been run. The two narrower
comparisons that are done both pass, with the same conclusions already
established for S1 and S5/b (this mechanism doesn't depend on the subsidy
scenario): clean divergence from `v1.1.0` and `v1.0.1`, correct
header/full-block asymmetry against the foreign `Aevust/rincoin` fork.

A fourth, non-automated comparison belongs in this section too: the
`rincoin-core/rincoin@v1.1` design review described above. It isn't a
pass/fail test, but it directly shaped what got built, and its finding (an
existing, structurally similar implementation that's actually unbounded)
is exactly the kind of evidence a "does this withstand real conditions"
report should carry.

Full detail: [`S6B/functional-test-results.md`](S6B/functional-test-results.md).
